screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Sports Medicine & Injury shortlist positions 13-24.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Personalized tendon loading reduces muscle‐tendon imbalances in male adolescent elite athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-six male elite adolescent handball athletes were followed across a season; 13 added individually prescribed patellar-tendon exercises three times weekly for about 31 weeks and 13 continued usual training. The intervention group increased knee-extensor strength and normalized patellar-tendon stiffness, had lower seasonal fluctuation in maximal tendon strain, and descriptively fewer athletes with strain at or above 9%; tendon structural-integrity and between-group strain changes were not significant.
records.limitations: The small, male, single-sport nonrandomized groups limit generalization and causal inference. It measured mechanical surrogate outcomes rather than tendon-injury incidence, and the specialized dynamometry, ultrasound, and tendon-strain prescription may not transfer directly to routine collegiate settings.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat individualized tendon-strain loading as a promising monitoring and training approach, not proof of tendon-injury prevention or a universal 4.5%-6.5% target. Progress loading with symptoms, clinical assessment, training exposure, and feasible measurement quality.

records.sourceFile: Clinical outcome following concussion among college athletes with a history of prior concussion - A systematic review.pdf
records.exclusionReason: The PDF is a 2025 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology scientific statement on competitive athletes with cardiovascular abnormalities (DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2024.12.025), not the queued systematic review of concussion outcomes. Source identity fails closed.

records.sourceFile: A systematic review of the relationship between workload and injury risk of professional male soccer players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This PRISMA review of professional male soccer literature through 2021 found that short-term fixture congestion appeared to increase match-injury incidence, whereas longer congestion showed no consistent overall or match-injury effect. It could not establish conclusive injury associations for GPS total distance, high-speed running, or acceleration; s-RPE acute:chronic workload ratio was associated with non-contact injury in some studies, but no minimum-risk threshold could be identified.
records.limitations: The review reports heterogeneous injury definitions, speed thresholds, GPS devices, analyses, and exposure windows, with relatively few GPS-injury studies. Its included evidence is observational and male professional soccer-specific, so apparent associations and ACWR thresholds do not establish causation or individual prediction.
records.synthesisCaution: Use workload data alongside availability, symptoms, recovery, exposure history, and sport context; do not set one GPS, s-RPE, ACWR, or fixture threshold as a clearance or injury-prediction rule.

records.sourceFile: The effects of fixture congestion on injury in professional male soccer - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Eight studies of professional male soccer defined congestion as at least two matches separated by four days or less. Five studies reported higher match-injury incidence in congested schedules, while findings for training and overall injury incidence varied; layoff duration was typically lower during congested periods.
records.limitations: The small evidence base used varying congestion definitions, injury definitions, scheduling contexts, and observational designs. Injury severity and exposure adjustment were inconsistent, and the evidence does not isolate fixture density from rotation, training modification, travel, or other club practices.
records.synthesisCaution: Flag congested periods for coordinated exposure, recovery, rotation, and symptom review, rather than infer that a four-day interval itself causes injury or prescribe a universal schedule restriction.

records.sourceFile: Time loss and recurrence of lateral ligament ankle sprains in male elite soccer - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This review identified 13 recurrence and 12 time-loss studies in male elite soccer. Random-effects pooling of 16,442 players estimated lateral-ankle-sprain recurrence at 17.11% (95% CI 13.31%-20.92%); time-loss data were too heterogeneous for pooling, with a descriptive weighted mean of 15.92 days and median 14.95 days.
records.limitations: Time-loss heterogeneity was considerable (I2 93%), and injury definitions, recurrence windows, severity reporting, and study designs differed. The findings are male elite soccer estimates, not individualized healing or return-to-competition criteria.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the short typical absence and recurrence burden to resist time-only progression; pair clinical status, function, sport exposure, and athlete-reported confidence when planning lateral-ankle-sprain return.

records.sourceFile: A rehabilitation algorithm after lateral ankle sprains in professional soccer - An approach based on clinical practice guidelines.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This clinical commentary presents a four-level lateral-ankle-sprain rehabilitation algorithm for professional soccer. Progression requires a level-dependent ankle-function score, standardized clinical examination, and functional-performance tests; it integrates current guideline assessments and interval kicking progression rather than relying on calendar time alone.
records.limitations: It is a Level 5 clinical commentary and proposed algorithm, not an effectiveness trial. Several phase-sensitive tests and criteria have not been evaluated for sensitivity, specificity, or reinjury reduction, and it is tailored to professional soccer resources.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the algorithm as a structured multidisciplinary checklist and adapt it to the athlete, setting, and medical plan. Do not represent its thresholds or progression sequence as validated predictors of safe return.

records.sourceFile: Short-term change on physical capacities of football players within few days before ACL-injury - A retrospective case-control study.pdf
records.exclusionReason: The PDF is a randomized trial of high-load versus low-load shoulder strengthening in patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder (DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2021-105223), not the queued retrospective ACL-injury case-control study. Source identity fails closed.

records.sourceFile: Acute-chronic workload ratio of professional soccer players preceding hamstring muscle injuries - A 2-season retrospective study.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In a two-season retrospective review of one professional male soccer team, 48 players generated 20 hamstring injuries. Before the injurious training or match exposure, 15 injuries (75%) had acute:chronic workload ratio below 1.5 for total distance, high-speed distance, very-high-speed distance, and actions above 19 km/h; only five players exceeded 1.5 for very-high-speed distance.
records.limitations: The study included only injury cases from one team, without uninjured exposure controls or prospective prediction testing. GPS workload omitted gym-based training, and the 1.5 cutoff, four-week window, and external-load metrics may not represent individual total load or tissue readiness.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not use an ACWR danger zone as the primary availability decision. Interpret workload trends with clinical status, high-speed exposure tolerance, prior injury, and the rest of the athlete's training.

records.sourceFile: Muscle fibre typology as a novel risk factor for hamstring strain injuries in professional soccer - A prospective cohort study.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across three seasons, the study estimated muscle-fibre typology noninvasively by soleus carnosine spectroscopy in professional Belgian and English soccer players. In the combined prospective cohort, fast typology was associated with 5.3-fold higher index hamstring-strain risk than slow typology (95% CI 1.92-14.8), based on 27 injuries.
records.limitations: This observational association involved relatively few injuries, male professional soccer players, and a soleus-based proxy for broader muscle typology rather than direct hamstring biopsy. It does not show that typology is modifiable or that screening and altering training from this result prevents injury.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat fibre typology, if measured with valid specialist methods, as one possible risk-context signal rather than a clearance label or deterministic injury forecast. Prioritize modifiable capacity, exposure, and clinical factors.

records.sourceFile: A musculoskeletal multifactorial individualized program for hamstring muscle injury risk reduction in professional - Results of a prospective cohort study.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Finnish premier-league teams used 2019 as control and a 2021 individualized multifactorial hamstring-risk program. Ninety control-season and 87 intervention-season players had 20 and 16 hamstring injuries, respectively; the primary time-to-injury comparison was not significant (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.39-1.51), while secondary analyses in the 31 players who completed both seasons found lower injury burden (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.85) and associations between compliance and lower incidence.
records.limitations: The nonrandomized previous-season control assumes exchangeable seasons; COVID-related disruption, club implementation differences, small samples, and possible underpowering limit causal inference. Positive secondary and compliance associations do not overturn the nonsignificant primary analysis.
records.synthesisCaution: A multifactorial program may be feasible, but retain the primary null result. Use individualized strength, sprint-exposure, range-of-motion, lumbopelvic, and monitoring work as a locally evaluated system rather than a proven injury-prevention package.

records.sourceFile: Jones fractures in elite athletes—2025 international foot and ankle sports consensus and systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A modified-Delphi panel generated 37 Jones-fracture statements and paired them with a systematic review of 27 studies (1,056 athletes). Stress-aetiology fractures were mainly treated with open reduction internal fixation (86.4%) with mean return to sport 13.3 plus or minus 4.5 weeks and 8.4% complications; traumatic fractures returned at 11.6 plus or minus 2.2 weeks regardless of treatment, while reported failure was highest in conservatively treated traumatic fractures (16.1%).
records.limitations: The consensus is Level V and much underlying evidence is nonrandomized, with treatment selection, fracture chronicity, athlete level, and return criteria varying. Some statements lacked supporting clinical data, and the expert process cannot eliminate bias.
records.synthesisCaution: Use imaging, fracture aetiology, displacement, healing, sport demand, and shared specialist decision-making; averages and consensus statements should not become a fixed return-to-sport timeline or automatic operative indication.

records.sourceFile: Evidence-based hamstring injury prevention and risk factor management - A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This review and meta-analysis of 108 parallel-group randomized trials in noninjured adult sport participants found eccentric training reduced hamstring-injury incidence by 56.8%-70.0%. Eccentric training improved concentric strength (MD 14.29 Nm), eccentric strength (MD 26.94 Nm), fascicle length (MD 0.90 cm), functional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, and strength asymmetry; static stretching improved flexibility more than PNF or dynamic stretching but its effects were more transient.
records.limitations: Nineteen trials raised some risk-of-bias concerns and seven were high risk, commonly from randomization or missing data; participant blinding was largely impossible. English-only searching and heterogeneity in interventions, outcomes, and populations restricted pooling and do not establish one optimal protocol.
records.synthesisCaution: Use eccentric loading as one component of progressive hamstring preparation, matched to capacity and sport exposure. Do not assume the pooled injury reduction selects a single exercise, dose, or solution for an individual athlete.
